title: Amos
subtitle: a herdsman, a priest, and a plumb line at Bethel
lead: Amos is among the earliest of the prophets whose words fill a whole book. He came from Tekoa in Judah, spoke in the northern kingdom at the shrine of Bethel in the long peace of Jeroboam II, and said that the LORD, who had brought Israel out of Egypt, would bring a foreign army against it. His charge was not about idols first; it was about what the rich did to the poor: debt slavery, bribery, false weights, worship that left the courts untouched.

The book moves from the LORD's roar from Zion (1:2), through judgment on seven nations and then on Israel, three sermons that begin "Hear this word", five visions, and a short story of the priest Amaziah ordering Amos to leave. It ends with five verses of restoration: the fallen booth of David raised up, the harvest overflowing, and Israel planted in its land. Whether Amos himself ended on hope is one of the book's chief debates.
facts: Amos, a herdsman and a tender of sycamore figs from Tekoa in Judah (1:1; 7:14). The book in its present form was put together by editors, and how much they added is debated.
Two years before an earthquake, in the days of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel (1:1); about 760 BC. The fall of Samaria in 722/721 BC lies ahead of the words.
The northern kingdom of Israel at the height of its wealth and peace; the shrine of Bethel (7:13) and the capital Samaria; Assyria is not named but is behind 5:27 and 6:14.
Oracles in poetry, with a few prose passages (7:1-17; 8:1-3); visions; funeral songs; woes; three hymns of praise; a closing promise.
The English and Hebrew verse numbers agree throughout; the Greek follows the Hebrew order, with the differences noted in the variants.

Third of the Twelve (the Minor Prophets, counted as one scroll in the Hebrew Bible) in the Masoretic order: Hosea, Joel, Amos. The Greek Bible places Amos second, after Hosea, and before Micah and Joel.
authorship: The book is the work of Amos, as the title says. Jewish and Christian tradition took the whole book, including 9:11-15, as his. Some conservative commentators still defend the whole book as one man's work (Andersen and Freedman, Paul, Hayes on large parts).

Most modern scholars think the core is Amos's own, but that later editors in Judah added to it (the Judah oracle 2:4-5, the hymns 4:13; 5:8-9; 9:5-6, the wisdom saying of 5:13 and the call to seek in 5:14-15 and the epilogue 9:11-15). Wolff and Jeremias give detailed stages of growth; Coggins and others are more careful. Even the claim that the book was edited by Amos's own disciples is a theory.

audience.to: The people of the northern kingdom of Israel in the reign of Jeroboam II, above all those who came to the shrine of Bethel and who lived in Samaria; the rich who ran the courts and the markets, and the poor who suffered. Judah is also in view (2:4-5; 6:1), and the readers of the book after 722 BC, in Judah, were the first to read the whole.
audience.why: Amos answered a people who thought they were safe: the nation was rich and at peace, the shrines were full, and the day of the LORD was a hope. His words say that the LORD's choice of Israel makes its debts heavier (3:2), that worship without justice is hateful to him (5:21-24), and that the army that will end the peace is already on the way. Knowing the audience changes the reading: on one reading the oracles against the nations are a trap, the cows of Bashan are most likely real women of Samaria, and the sermons are against a prosperity that looked like blessing.
views: Most scholars imagine the book rests on speeches at Bethel and Samaria in a short period (Wolff, Paul).
Some think the book was made for readers, mostly in Judah, after 722 BC, who needed an explanation of the fall of the north (Jeremias).
Hayes and others hold that Amos prophesied at Bethel, and that the book was shaped later for new readers.

outline: Title and motto: the LORD roars from Zion
Oracles against the nations: Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab, Judah, Israel
First sermon: "You only have I known"; the questions; Samaria's citadels
Second sermon: cows of Bashan; Bethel; five disasters; "get ready to meet your God"; hymn
A lament and a call: "Seek me and live"; hymn; the gate
Woe on those who long for the day of the LORD; the hated festivals; "let justice roll"
Third sermon: woe on the comfortable; the pride of Jacob; Lo-debar
Visions 1 to 3: locusts, fire, the plumb line
Vision 4: summer fruit; buying the poor; the famine of hearing
Vision 5: the Lord beside the altar; hymn; Cushites; sifting
Epilogue: the fallen booth of David and the harvest of restoration

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Amos of Tekoa at Bethel in the long peace of Jeroboam II and Uzziah (2 Kings 14:23-29; 2 Chronicles 26), two years before the earthquake; land accumulation, debt slavery, bribery and false weights; the Assyrian threat; the fall of Samaria in 722/721 BC.

lenses.name: Critical scholarship
lenses.desc: Composition: the prophet's own oracles and the Judean additions argued for 1:9-12, 2:4-5, the hymns and 9:11-15 (Wolff, Jeremias, Paul, Andersen-Freedman, Hayes, Coggins); the rhetoric of the nation oracles; the visions; the date of 1:1; the Hebrew, the Greek and the scrolls.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The Targum Jonathan; the medieval commentators Rashi, Radak (Kimhi) and Ibn Ezra, read only for the verses cited (in the text on Sefaria; Rashi's commentary on Amos is only partly preserved there, and the three were not read through); the Talmud (Makkot 23b-24a on "Seek me and live"; Sanhedrin 96b-97a on Bar Nafle); the Damascus Document at Qumran; the book as one of the Twelve. The haftarot are not cited (not checked).

lenses.name: Christian tradition
lenses.desc: Acts 7:42-43 and Acts 15:15-18; Jerome, Cyril, Theodoret and Theodore of Mopsuestia on the Twelve; Luther and Calvin; the social gospel; Martin Luther King Jr. on 5:24; Catholic social teaching; liberation theology; Quaker and Anabaptist readings. The readings of Jerome, Cyril, Theodoret, Theodore, Luther and Calvin on Amos were not checked for this book, so no view is attributed to them.

lenses.name: Still to come
lenses.desc: The day of the LORD (5:18-20), the booth of David (9:11) and the restoration (9:13-15) as read by dispensational, amillennial, progressive dispensational and Jewish writers.

sections.b:
Amos is best read as a set of speeches and visions in a short sequence, from the roar of the lion in 1:2 to the sermon on the comfortable in chapter 6, and then the visions. The units that begin "Hear this word" (3:1; 4:1; 5:1) mark the three sermons, and the "Woe" of 5:18 and 6:1 divides the rest. Read the oracles against the nations (1:3-2:16) as a single piece: on one reading the first six get the crowd to agree, and the last two turn on the crowd.

Amos mixes prose and poetry. The visions of 7:1-9 and the Amaziah story (7:10-17) are in prose (with the oracle of 7:9 in poetry, and the quoted speech of 7:11 and 7:16-17 in prose); the sermons are in poetry. The Plain marks the poetry with " / ".

The center of the book is the claim that the LORD cares about how people treat one another. Amos names the crimes in detail: selling the poor for a pair of sandals (2:6; 8:6), trampling their heads in the dust (2:7), keeping a poor person's coat as a pledge (2:8), taking bribes at the gate (5:12), cheating with a small measure and a heavy weight (8:5). The law behind these charges is in Exodus 21-23 and Deuteronomy 24-25. Amos does not make up a new law; he holds Israel to the one it has. And he says that worship cannot cover for injustice (5:21-24). The prophets are not against sacrifice (Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6-8 say the same), and the book is not a modern political program; it is a covenant lawsuit.

The first prophet in whose book the phrase appears, Amos finds the day of the LORD already expected by his hearers (5:18). They long for it as a day of victory. He says it is darkness. For him the day is near and historical: an invading army. Later prophets use the phrase for the fall of Jerusalem (Zephaniah 1; Joel) and for the last judgment, and the New Testament for the return of Christ. See the topic page.

Two verses hold the book's thought on election. Amos 3:2 says that out of all the clans of the earth the LORD has known Israel only, and so will call it to account: being chosen is a weight. "Are you Israelites not like the Cushites to me?" (Amos 9:7) and the questions about the Philistines from Caphtor and the Arameans from Kir say that the exodus is not the LORD's only act of leading a people. The oracles against the nations (1:3-2:3) add that all nations are held to account for how they treat others. Jewish and Christian readers have drawn different conclusions from these verses; see the cards on the chapter pages.

sections.h: The Hebrew, the Greek and the scrolls
sections.b: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text (the Leningrad Codex). The Greek Amos (the Septuagint) differs in many verses; the notable ones are 3:9, 3:11, 3:12, 4:13, 5:8, 5:26, 6:2, 6:12, 7:1, 8:3, 8:8, 8:14 and 9:11-12. Amos is preserved at Qumran in 4QXIIc (4Q78), 4QXIIg (4Q82) and 5QAmos (5Q4), and in the Murabba'at scroll of the Twelve (Mur88), which is in the Masoretic tradition. The transcriptions of Abegg, Bowley and Cook show that these scrolls agree with the Masoretic Text in nearly every place, including 9:12 in Mur88, where the word "Edom" stands. In several places the scrolls are broken exactly where the question lies (6:12, 7:1, 8:14), and the variants say so rather than cite a restored word. The variants section gives each reading.

sections.h: Amos in the New Testament and after
sections.b: Stephen quotes 5:25-27 in the Greek (Acts 7:42-43) and James quotes 9:11-12 in the Greek (Acts 15:15-18). The darkness at noon of 8:9 has often been linked to Matthew 27:45. Martin Luther King Jr. used 5:24 at the March on Washington in 1963. Catholic social teaching, the social gospel, liberation theology, and Quaker and Anabaptist writers have all drawn on Amos. Readers should keep in mind that Amos spoke to a particular people in a particular time; each later use is a reading, and the cards and notes label them.

spec.title: Five curses and five visions
spec.body: My own observation: the book has two sets of five. In 4:6-11 the LORD sends five disasters, each ending "yet you did not turn back to me". In 7:1-9:4 there are five visions: locusts, fire, plumb line, summer fruit, and the Lord beside the altar. In the first set the people never respond. In the second set the prophet prays twice and is heard, and then no prayer is possible. It looks as if the five visions are the answer to the five refusals. This overlaps with the observation by Wolff and others that the visions have a pattern of 2 + 2, and I do not know of a published argument that links the two sets.

prompts: The herdsman at the gate of Bethel

A drawing sketched onto an old scroll in ink and ochre: a lean man with a shepherd's staff and a basket of small figs standing before the carved gateway of a hilltop shrine, a priest in a long robe pointing him away, soft smudged edges, in the style of ancient manuscript mixed with cave drawing and modern line art, no hard rectangles.
The plumb line and the wall

A hand-drawn image on parchment: a tall wall of rough stones and a weight on a cord hanging beside it, a faint figure at the top of the wall with a lantern, charcoal lines and washes of earth color, soft edges that fade into the scroll.

An ink and ochre sketch on a scroll: a woven basket of ripe figs and pomegranates in the foreground, and behind it the outline of a city of ivory-colored houses with a crack running through it, in the manner of cave drawing and ancient manuscript illustration, soft edges.
reading: Hans Walter Wolff, Joel and Amos (Hermeneia)
The standard critical commentary on the growth of the book in stages.
A close reading of the Hebrew with ancient Near Eastern background; defends much of the book for Amos.
Francis Andersen and David Noel Freedman, Amos (Anchor Bible)
A large commentary with a long discussion of the text and the theory that the book is mostly Amos's.
John H. Hayes, Amos the Eighth-Century Prophet
A historical reading of Amos in his time.
Jorg Jeremias, The Book of Amos (Old Testament Library)
A compact commentary on the stages of the book.
Richard Coggins, Joel and Amos (New Century Bible)
A shorter commentary that compares the views.
A classic on the prophets' sense of God's pathos, with chapters on justice.
